questions.enonce_markdown: What is the religious importance of medicine men in African Traditional Religions? (25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** In African Traditional Religions the medicine man (or woman) is a specialist who heals, protects and communicates with the spiritual world. He is called by different names (traditional healer, herbalist, diviner, doctor), and these are generalities that vary among peoples. Mbiti and other writers regard him as one of the most important religious figures in the community.

**1. A healer of body and spirit.** The medicine man uses herbs, roots, barks and other remedies with prayers and rituals. Illness is seen as having physical, social and spiritual aspects, so healing deals with the whole person and not only with the symptoms.

**2. A diviner.** He discovers the cause of misfortune, such as sickness, barrenness, accident, death or drought, through divination (casting objects, reading signs, consulting spirits, dreams). He says whether the cause is a broken taboo, an offended ancestor, a spirit or the action of a witch or sorcerer, and he prescribes the remedy, often a sacrifice or a rite.

**3. An intermediary.** He is believed to communicate with spirits, divinities and ancestors, sometimes in a state of possession or trance, and to pass their messages to the community. He may direct sacrifices and offerings.

**4. A protector against evil.** He protects people, homes and farms from witchcraft, sorcery and evil spirits by means of charms, amulets and cleansing rites. He is also consulted for success in farming, hunting, trading and the protection of children.

**5. A guardian of the moral order.** By discovering offences and prescribing reconciliation or purification, he helps keep harmony in society. His role is distinct from that of the sorcerer, who is believed to use power against others. The medicine man is regarded as using power for good, although the boundary can be unclear to outsiders.

**6. A keeper of knowledge and counsellor.** He keeps knowledge of plants, healing and customs which is passed on through apprenticeship, often by a family or by a call from the spirits. People bring their personal and family troubles to him, so he is also a counsellor.

**7. Evaluation.** The medicine man is important because he addresses the African view that the spiritual and physical are one. Today many people also use modern hospitals, and the position of the medicine man has changed. Critics warn about fraud and the risk of harmful remedies, and churches and mosques have at times opposed some practices. Yet the medicine man remains influential.

**Conclusion.** The religious importance of medicine men in ATR lies in their roles as healers, diviners, intermediaries, protectors against evil and guardians of knowledge and order. They link the visible and the invisible worlds and help to keep the community in balance.
